Large fractionations of C and H isotopes related to methane oxidation in Arctic lakes Sarah B. Cadieux a,*, Jeffrey R. White b, Peter E. Sauer a, Yongbo Peng a,1, Amy E. Goldman a,b,2, Lisa M. Pratt a a Department of Geological Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA b School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA Received 14 November 2015; accepted in revised form 3 May 2016; available online 9 May 2016 Abstract Microbial oxidation of methane (CH4) plays a central role in carbon cycling in Arctic lakes, reducing potential CH4 emissions associated with warming. Isotopic signatures of CH4 (δ13C and δ2H) are indicators of microbial oxidation, wherein the process strongly enriches 13C and 2H in residual CH4. We present δ13C and δ2H measurements obtained from sampling the water column and sediment for dissolved CH4 from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland under both open-water and ice-covered conditions from 2013 to 2014. Despite substantial variations in aquatic chemistry among the lakes, δ13C and δ2H of CH4 suggested that CH4 was produced predominantly by acetoclastic methanogenesis in the littoral sediments and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. Surprisingly large variations for both δ13C and δ2H of CH4 were observed, with δ13C extending from −72‰ to +7.4‰ and δ2H from −390‰ to +250‰. The CH4 isotopic values reported here were significantly more enriched (p < 0.0001) in both 13C and 2H than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments. As is characteristic of methanotrophy, the enrichment in 13C and 2H was associated with low CH4 concentrations. We suggest that the CH4 most enriched in 13C and 2H may reflect unusually efficient methanotrophic communities in Arctic ice-margin lakes. This study provides the first measurement of δ2H for CH4 in an Arctic freshwater environment at concentrations <10 μM. The extreme enrichment of 13C and 2H of CH4 from Arctic methanotrophy has significant implications for interpreting sources and sinks of CH4. Without knowledge of local geology, stable isotope values of CH4 higher than −30‰ for δ13C and −150‰ for δ2H could be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic origins. Given crystalline bedrock and the strong positive correlation between δ13C and δ2H throughout the water columns in three Arctic lakes confirms that CH4 heavily enriched in 13C and 2H is the result of methanotrophy. Keywords: Methane; Hydrogen isotopes; Carbon isotopes; Arctic; Lakes 1. INTRODUCTION Small lakes (<10 km^2) represent approximately half of the total area of surface water in Arctic environments (Abnizova et al., 2012) and emit more methane (CH4) per unit area than larger lakes (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009; Downing, 2010). Microbial oxidation of CH4 is an important process in freshwater ecosystems, reincorporating CH4 back into the biogeochemical carbon cycle rather than being released as CH4 into the atmosphere. In northern lakes, up to 88% of the CH4 produced by microbes is oxidized by methanotrophs (Kankaala et al., 2006, 2007; Bastviken et al., 2008; López Bellido et al., 2009), leaving low concentrations of CH4 in surface water of lakes. Due to the challenge of reliably measuring stable isotope abundances at very low concentrations, the effect of methanotrophic oxidation on isotopes of CH4 in Arctic lakes has not previously been reported. The combination of concentration and isotopic signature is vital for understanding biogeochemical cycling of CH4 on Earth and for assessing pathways for production and oxidation of CH4 on Mars where episodic plumes of CH4 at low concentrations have been detected remotely and measured by instruments on martian rovers. In anticipation of returning samples from Mars to Earth and with increasing interest in astronauts as explorers on Mars, it is urgent to assess geochemical and/or biological processes influencing rates of CH4 formation and destruction (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Kinetic isotope effects associated with enzymatic processes during methanogenesis and methanotrophy are well established terrestrial biomarkers and are potential martian biomarkers for subsurface life. Measuring CH4 concentrations and CH4 fluxes are useful to assess the magnitude of emissions, but alone are unable to be used to decipher active production and pathways. Stable isotopic analysis of carbon (δ13C) and hydrogen (δ2H) is a well-established method to delineate the origin of CH4 gas, allowing for the differentiation of CH4 produced by microbial and thermal processes as well as microbial production and oxidation (Schoell, 1980; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Despite a wide range of literature using 13C and 2H to interpret origin and thermal maturity of hydrocarbons in petroleum systems (Stahl and Carey, 1975; Schoell, 1980, 1988; Whiticar, 1989; Jackson et al., 2014), there has been limited work on δ13C and δ2H of CH4 in natural environments, most of which has been focused on wetlands (Martens et al., 1992; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Sugimoto and Fujita, 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). Biogenic CH4 in freshwater environments is produced predominantly within anoxic sediments and is exported into the water column by ebullition (bubbling) or diffusion (Strayer and Tiedje, 1978; Bastviken et al., 2008). Microbial CH4 is produced by methanogens, strictly anaerobic Archaea, who are responsible for 10–50% of overall carbon mineralization in freshwater lakes (Bastviken et al., 2008). In freshwater environments, there are two primary metabolic pathways for CH4 production, acetoclastic methanogenesis (AM) and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM), which have been demonstrated to vary spatially in permafrost-influenced ecosystems (Prater et al., 2007). Both AM and HM are associated with a kinetic isotope effect resulting in depletion of 13C in the product CH4 relative to the pre-cursor substrate (Whiticar et al., 1986; Balabane et al., 1987; Valentine et al., 2004a,b). However, the magnitude of the carbon isotope effect is different for the two primary methanogenic pathways, with AM resulting in δ13CCH4 ranging from −60‰ to −40‰, and HM ranging from −110‰ to −60‰ (Whiticar et al., 1986). Hydrogen isotopes of CH4 similarly become depleted in 2H during microbial CH4 production. The δ2H value of CH4 depends on the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is either from cleavage of H2O or acetate (Woltemate et al., 1984; Whiticar, 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Although this remains contentious, it is generally assumed that during HM, all 4 H atoms are supplied by formation water, whereas during AM, the transfer of the methyl group to CH4 supplies 3 H atoms, and the additional H atom is derived from formation water (Whiticar et al., 1986). As a result, the magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect of hydrogen is different for the two pathways, dependent on value of precursor δ2H, with AM resulting in δ2HCH4 ranging from −530‰ to −250‰, and HM ranging from −250‰ to −170‰ (Sugimoto and Wada, 1995). The isotope systematics of hydrogen for homoacetogenesis in competition with methanogenesis under substrate-limiting conditions and low temperatures of natural systems is not well known (Kotsyurbenko et al., 2001), although culture studies suggest that there is rapid hydrogen isotope exchange between H2 and H2O during homoacetogenesis (Valentine et al., 2004a,b). Methane oxidation (MOx) depends on both the availability of CH4 and dissolved oxygen (DO); high CH4 oxidation rates are usually found at the oxic/anoxic interface where both CH4 and DO are abundant (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) can also occur by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors in lieu of dissolved oxygen (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). High affinity methanotrophs are able to oxidize CH4 at or below atmospheric concentrations (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Isotope fractionation associated with microbial CH4 oxidation leads to systematic enrichment in both 13C and 2H of CH4 in the residual un-oxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). The enrichment in both 13C and 2H during oxidation results in values being increased by <1–30‰ for δ13CCH4 and 3–200‰ for δ2HCH4 (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Bastviken et al., 2002). In this study, we report values of δ13C and δ2H for CH4 collected from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland to assess seasonal sources and sinks of CH4. Lakes were sampled during open-water conditions in July 2013 and under ice-cover in April 2014 when the lakes had been ice-covered and isolated from the atmosphere for 7–8 months. The studied lakes show considerable variation in concentration and proportions of major ions despite being located along a 6 km segment of a narrow valley. Therefore, we hypothesize that due to chemical heterogeneity, sources and sinks of CH4 in each lake would vary lake-to-lake as well as seasonally. Hundreds of thousands of Holocene lakes dot the landscape in southwestern Greenland (Anderson et al., 2001; Anderson and Stedmon, 2007) and are underlain by continuous permafrost (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Deglaciation began in the region ~11,000 BP (Van Tatenhove and van der Meer, 1996; Leng et al., 2012), exposing Precambrian metamorphic crystalline bedrock, primarily felsic gneisses (Jensen et al., 2002). As a result, CH4 in these lakes has had little to no influence from buried ancient organic matter, allowing biogenic CH4 cycles to be studied in isolation. To our knowledge, this work provides the first coupled measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 under both open-water and ice-covered conditions in a relatively undisturbed, periglacial, lacustrine setting thereby filling critical knowledge gaps concerning biogeochemical cycles of CH4 within small Arctic lakes and isotope fractionation of CH4 in low concentration environments. 2. STUDY AREA Lakes in this study are located between the village of Kangerlussuaq, Greenland at the head of Søndre Strømfjord and the active terminus of the Russell Glacier (Fig. 1). During the last Glacial Maximum, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) covered the area. Retreat of the GIS likely resulted in formation of the lakes in glacially scoured hollows (Leng et al., 2012). Currently, the margin of the GIS is ~2 km away from the study lakes. The region has continuous permafrost <50 cm below the surface, extending down to 130 m at Kangerlussuaq and 500 m at the edge of the ice sheet (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Bedrock is predominantly garnet-grade, Archean gneisses with Quaternary glacial, fluvial and alluvial deposits present in low-lying areas. Mean annual air temperature at the Kangerlussuaq weather station from 1974 to 2012 was −6 °C. During warm months of late May to early September, mean temperatures often exceed +11 °C and peak to +20 °C in July. The cold season extends from November to late March, with mean daily temperature averaging −21 °C in February. Precipitation in the Kangerlussuaq area is minimal, with annual precipitation <150 mm yr−1, mostly from June to August (Ohmura and Reeh, 1991). Dwarf shrubs (Salix, Vaccinium and Betula), Sphagnum spp., and graminoids (Carex and Calamagrostis) dominate the tundra vegetation in the region. 2.1. Study lakes In this paper three, small adjacent lakes (surface area <3 ha, maximum depth <8 m) with a range of different morphometries and aquatic chemistries (Fig. 1; Table 1) are studied. Lake names used herein are informal names. The study lakes are part of a series of lakes within a narrow valley overlying a structural shear zone extending from the Russell Glacier to the Søndre Strømfjord (Fig. 1). The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (\( Z_{\text{max}} \)), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L\(^{-1}\)), pH, and specific conductivity (\( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column \( CH_4 \) collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and \( CH_4 \) was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved \( CH_4 \) in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment \( CH_4 \) Profundal sediment samples were taken from \( Z_{\text{max}} \) of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Sediment was collected in polycarbonate plastic barrels with an internal diameter of 6.7 cm. Dissolved gas in the sediment was sampled using an equilibrium gas stripping method similar to the water-column CH₄ (Section 3.1.2.1). Sediment cores were subsectioned into 6–10 cm intervals and put into 8 L Nalgene bottles, with lids altered to include two syringe ports connected to Luer-Lock fittings. Once the sediment was put into the bottle and the lid was shut, the bottle was evacuated using a hand pump connected to a lid port. After evacuation, zero-CH₄ water was injected to create a 4 L sediment–water slurry. The bottle was vigorously shaken for 5 min to displace gas from the sediment-slurry into the headspace. 3.1.4. Littoral sediment CH₄ Littoral sediment gas samples were collected during open-water conditions by physically disturbing the sediment in order to release entrained gas bubbles. Each sample was collected from a vegetated region where water depth was <0.5 m. Gas bubbles were collected using an inverted plastic funnel (28 cm diameter) with a gas-tight sampling tube and 3-way Luer-Lock valve attached to the neck. Gas in the funnel was transferred to a Cali-5-Bond bag using a plastic syringe. Note that we were unable to quantify the volume of sediment sampled. Consequently, concentrations of CH₄ in gas collected from littoral sediments cannot be converted into pool size of CH₄ in the littoral sediments. Rather, the samples were used to constrain the isotopic composition of CH₄ present in the littoral sediments (Chanton, 2005). 3.2. Laboratory methods 3.2.1. Concentration of CH₄ Concentration of water-column CH₄ and sediment CH₄ was measured using a Los Gatos Research (LGR) Methane Carbon Isotope Analyzer (MCIA) (LGR, Mountain View CA, USA) at the Kangerlussuaq International Science Support facility (KISS). The LGR MCIA is a portable, off-axis, integrated cavity output spectrometer that measures CH₄ without sample preparation. All samples were processed within 24 h of collection. For each analysis, 400–600 mL of gas sample was required. Calibration was repeated every 10 samples, with Scotty® gas standards of 50 and 100 ppmv CH₄. Samples were diluted with a known volume of zero-air in order to bring them within the range of the calibration gases. The total concentration of CH₄ in each sample was corrected for dilution and calculated from the sum of the measured headspace partial pressure and the dissolved CH₄ remaining after gas stripping, calculated according to Henry’s law using values after Lide and Fredrikse (1995). Instrumental uncertainty of CH₄ from the MCIA was ±0.5 ppmv, which is one standard deviation of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. Previously, concentrations of CH₄ from MCIA were analyzed on a Gas Chromatograph Flame Ionization Detector (GC-FID) to confirm validity (Appendix 2). Aliquots of each sample were transferred to pre-evacuated glass vials and returned to Indiana University, USA for carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄. 3.3. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄ Stable C and H isotopes of CH₄ were analyzed using two approaches. MCIA was used for C isotopic analysis on samples with CH₄ concentrations >50 ppmv, but the MCIA produces unreliable results at lower concentrations (Appendix 3). Therefore, stable isotope ratios of both carbon and hydrogen of CH₄ were measured using continuous-flow gas chromatography-oxidation/pyrolysis isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-ox/pyr-IRMS) with a laboratory-built gas pre-concentrator interfaced with a ThermoFinnigan GCC and Delta Plus XP IRMS at the Stable Isotope Research Facility (SIRF) at Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana. The pre-concentrator design was modeled after principles described by Merritt et al. (1995) and inlet system developed by Miller et al. (2002) for carbon isotope analysis and Brass and Rockmann (2010) for carbon and hydrogen isotopes. The gas sample containing CH₄ is first dried by passing through a cold trap and then passed into a stainless steel sample loop packed with HayeSep D and kept at −130 °C. After the CH₄ is extracted, the trap is warmed to −20 °C and the CH₄ is cryofocused at the head of Varian Porabond Q GC column. Carbon of CH₄ is converted to CO₂ at 950 °C and H is converted to H₂ in an alumina reactor at 1450 °C. Carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios are expressed in standard δ notation (δ¹³C and δ²H): \[ \delta = [(R_{\text{sample}} - R_{\text{standard}})/R_{\text{standard}}] \times 1000 = \%o \] where \( R \) is the molar ratio of heavy to light isotopes (¹³C/¹²C, ²H/¹H) for both sample and standard. Carbon isotope values are referenced to VPDB and hydrogen isotope values are referenced to VSMOW by comparison with pure CH₄ where the isotopic composition has been measured by off-line combustion (http://mypage.iu.edu/~aschimme/compounds.html). Instrumental uncertainty of δ¹³C and δ²H from the GC-C-IRMS was calculated as ±0.4‰ and as ±10‰ respectively, which is one standard deviation for repeated measures of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. 3.4. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were made using IBM SPSS Statistics. Combined concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic compositions for all study lakes during each season were assessed for normal distribution via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and were found to be non-normally distributed. Student’s t tests of unequal variance were used for testing statistically significant differences in concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic values of CH₄ between seasons and between study results and reported isotopic values from other natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude. Systematic changes in δ¹³C and δ²H were analyzed using linear regression, based upon the pathway of oxidation leading to systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of CH₄ in the residual unoxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). 4. RESULTS 4.1. Water-column CH₄ 4.1.1. Concentration of CH₄ Under open-water conditions, concentrations of CH₄ were strongly related to DO dynamics (Fig. 2). Dissolved CH₄ concentrations in the surface waters of the three lakes ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 µM (Fig. 3). Clinograde DO profiles were measured in EVV Upper and Potentilla lakes with DO saturated in surface water (9.5 and 11.0 mg L⁻¹ respectively), and decreasing with depth to anoxia (<0.5 mg L⁻¹; Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column with decreasing DO, with the maximum CH₄ observed in the anoxic water at the sediment–water interface (150 and 67 µM respectively). Teardrop lake was oxic to suboxic (DO > 1 mg L⁻¹) throughout the water column with an oxygen anomaly at 4.0 m, wherein DO drastically shifted from >10 mg L⁻¹ at 3.5 m to 1.8 mg L⁻¹ at 4 m, and then returned to 7 mg L⁻¹ at 4.5 m. Throughout the water column of Teardrop lake, there were low CH₄ concentrations (<8.1 µM; Fig. 3). In all three lakes, concentrations of CH₄ were significantly greater under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (n = 31, p = 0.0002). A downward increase in CH₄ concentration from below ice-cover to the sediment–water interface was measured in all three lakes under ice-covered conditions (Fig. 3). Potentilla lake was the only lake with measurable DO under ice-cover (Fig. 3). Consequently, CH₄ concentrations dynamically followed DO with highest concentrations (220 µM) observed within the anoxic bottom waters and decreasing concentrations tracking increasing dissolved DO upward through the water column until concentrations of CH₄ reached levels <1 µM immediately below the ice (Fig. 3). EVV Upper and Teardrop lakes were entirely anoxic below ice-cover with concentrations of CH₄ >50 µM throughout the water column (Fig. 3). 4.1.2. \( \delta^{13}C \) of water-column CH₄ Under open-water conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the three lakes ranged from −68.7‰ to +7.4‰ (Fig. 3). Isotopic evidence of production pathways for CH4 in Greenlandic lakes Bedrock in the Kangerlussuaq region consists of tightly folded, felsic gneisses exposed to garnet-grade metamorphism and contains no measurable organic C, therefore we assume that all CH4 within the study lakes is biologically produced. To look at differences in microbial production of CH4, we focus our discussion on the sediment CH4 in the study lakes from open-water conditions. In order to distinguish AM and HM CH4 production pathways from each other isotopically, isotopic compositions of H2O, dissolved inorganic matter (DIC), and organic matter (OM) must be constant. If not, the variation in δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 reflect not only different production pathways, but also variation in environmental factors that affect isotopic composition of reactants. In the study lakes, δ2H2O in the water column slightly decreases with distance away from the margin of the GIS, from a median of −91.5‰ in EVV Upper lake to −97.4‰ in Potentilla lake. Despite the spatial variation in δ2H2O among the lakes, there is no significant relationship between δ2H2O from the water column and δ2HCH4 from sediments (Fig. 5), suggesting that δ2HCH4 is not a direct reflection of variation in 2H2O. In addition to differences in δ2H2O among the lakes, there are also variations in δ13CDIC from the water column among the lakes (Stern et al., 2014). However, there is not enough data to confirm or deny if δ13CCH4 is reflecting variation in δ13CDIC. Approximately a 5‰ difference in δ13COM of particulate OM from profundal sediments was observed lake-to-lake, ranging from −29.2‰ in EVV Upper lake to −24.5‰ (Table 1). Data suggest that the ~45‰ difference in δ13CCH4 of profundal sediment may reflect the δ13COM of precursor OM (Fig. 5b). However, the range in δ13COM is narrow compared to the overall range observed in aquatic chemistry and δ13CCH4 among the lakes. In both the profundal and littoral sediments of the study lakes, values of δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 are consistent with microbial CH4 production (Fig. 4) (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Profundal sediment CH4 is more depleted in 13C and enriched in 2H relative to littoral sediment CH4 (Table 2), suggesting different microbial production pathways, partial oxidation of the littoral sediments, or higher precursor δ13COM in the littoral sediments. However, δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 values from both profundal and littoral sediments plot primarily within the AM field (Fig. 4). The HM pathway field in the δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 classification diagram was determined from marine samples where δ2H2O is ~0‰ (Whiticar, 1999; Waldron et al., 1999b). As a result, the HM pathway field may not accurately represent Arctic waters where δ2H2O ≪ 0‰. Using the assumptions from Chanton et al. (2006), we can adjust the measured sediment δ2HCH4 for the δ2H2O of the water in the lake where the CH4 was formed using the following equation: \[ \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-measured}} - \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\text{ water}} = \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-adjusted}} \] In order to use this equation, δ2HCH4 in the sediments must reflect CH4 production without isotopic overprinting from oxidation. If CH4 in the sediments was subjected to oxidation then a positive correlation between δ13CCH4 and δ²HCH₄ would be observed (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). An inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ from sediments, confirming CH₄ in the sediments had not been oxidized (Fig. 4). The adjustment for δ²H₂O shifted δ²HCH₄ of profundal sediments into the HM pathways field, whereas the littoral sediment δ²HCH₄ remains primarily in the AM pathway field (Fig. 6). Without δ¹³COM in the littoral sediments of each lake, we are unable to assess if the variations between the sediments are the result of different microbial pathways, or if there is also variations in precursor OM. However, δ¹³COM and C/N ratios of littoral sediments from EVV Upper lake suggested OM is sourced from in-lake primary production (Thompson, 2015). The difference in CH₄ production pathway between the littoral and profundal sediments likely reflects the supply of labile organic compounds and δ¹³COM, which would influence CH₄ formation (Duc et al., 2010). In the littoral sediments, aquatic macrophytes and phytoplankton supply a source of labile OM, resulting in AM. Correspondingly, the lake with the highest CH₄ concentrations in the littoral sediments (EVV Upper lake) has the highest concentration of aquatic macrophytes, with the shoreline dominated by Hippuris vulgaris. In freshwater environments, CH₄ typically is produced by AM (Whiticar et al., 1986; Conrad, 1999) because plant root exudates and fresh OM provide a ready supply of labile OM to the bacteria. Previous theoretical values predict that HM accounts for ~30% of overall CH₄ production in freshwater lakes (Conrad, 1999). In high-latitude Sphagnum bogs, CH₄ production via HM is dominant because of an inhibition of the AM pathway, whereas AM is dominant in Carex-rich environments (Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Sphagnum spp. was a significant component of littoral communities of lakes in this study. In closed lake basins, OM from these areas may represent important carbon inputs, which could be influencing the HM pathway for CH₄ production in the profundal sediments. We were surprised to discover that despite significant variations in DOC, SO₄²⁻ and conductivity among the lakes, formation pathways of CH₄ in littoral and profundal sediments seem to be identical in all of the lakes. Competition for substrates (particularly acetate and H₂) favors sulfate reduction (SR), inhibiting CH₄ production (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Ward and Winfrey, 1985; Scholten et al., 2002). Methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased because SR can very effectively uptake both H₂ and acetate, maintaining H₂ and acetate concentrations too low for methanogens (Lovely and Klung, 1986). In the study lakes, EVV Upper lake has the highest SO₄²⁻ concentrations and is the only lake with detectable H₂S in the water column during open-water conditions (Table 1). The presence and accumulation of CH₄ in the sediments indicates that there is sufficient carbon to both fuel reduction of the SO₄²⁻ pool and support methanogenesis in EVV Upper lake. Given the current data, there is no way to assess if communities are spatially coexisting or separated by vertical stratification. However, EVV Upper lake does have the lowest concentration of CH₄ in the profundal sediments, which could be due to SR reducing methanogenesis. Isotopic evidence of consumption of CH₄ by methanotrophic oxidation Under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, concentrations of CH₄ are strongly related to dissolved oxygen dynamics, suggesting MOx is reducing water column CH₄. Methane can also be consumed under anoxic conditions, by AOM (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). However, the strong relationship between CH₄ and DO suggests that in the lakes here, aerobic MOx is the dominant pathway consuming CH₄. Oxidation of CH₄ leads to a systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of the residual un-oxidized CH₄ (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). In the profundal and littoral sediments of all of the lakes, an inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄, suggesting the CH₄ has not been fully oxidized. In the water column under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, a strong, positive correlation between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ is observed in all the lakes (\( n = 51, R = 0.93, p < 0.001 \); Fig. 2c), indicating CH₄ has been oxidized. In oxic waters, CH₄ is systematically enriched in both ¹³C and ²H, which is consistent with MOx (Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Happell et al., 1994; Whiticar, 1999; Bastviken et al., 2002; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). The slope of enrichment of ¹³C and 2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly. Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994): \[ f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000) \] where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx. The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014). 5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported. The shaded area denotes the field of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) associated with microbial CH$_4$ production (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) 5.4. Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed. The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (\( Z_{\text{max}} \)), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L\(^{-1}\)), pH, and specific conductivity (\( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column \( CH_4 \) collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and \( CH_4 \) was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved \( CH_4 \) in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Seasonal productivity in beds of submerged macrophytes is predicted by the TP measured during previous winter but even if this single test is significant (\( r^2 = 0.932, p = 0.034 \)), the \( p \) value was above the corrected value of \( \alpha \) for multiple tests (see Table 6). The \( r^2 \) and significance of the linear regressions between productivity rates by subset of measures depending on the location and physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 6. 3.2. Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself.
